summary: Portabello and summer squash lasagna: thin slices of squash and portabello caps (cut on the bias) fried until well browned, layered with no-boil noodles, lemony tomato sauce, nutmeg ricotta and mozzarella, baked at 375°F (covered 30 minutes, then about 30 more) until 170°F inside; serves 8 in 90 minutes.
glance: 375°F, covered 30 minutes, then about 30 more until 170°F inside
9 x 13 inches, at least 2 inches deep, about 4 layers
faq: Why this lasagna instead of spinach and ricotta?
The two most common vegetarian lasagnas are filled with spinach and ricotta, or with piles of watery vegetables. This version with portabello and summer squash gives a much more decisive flavor.
How do I slice the portobellos?
Pull off the stems and lay the caps flat, then hold your knife at an angle and cut through them on the bias into 1/8-inch slabs with as much surface area as possible.
What are no-boil lasagna noodles?

The same as any other dried pasta, just rolled a little thinner so they cook through in the oven. Make sure they're surrounded with enough sauce to absorb so they soften as they cook; regular noodles should be par-boiled.
How do I keep the lasagna from being watery?
Fry the squash and portabellos in a single layer over high heat until well browned on both sides and drain them on paper towels before layering.
How do I know it's done?

Internal temperature of 170°F, or you can easily pierce the noodles with a fork and the sauce is bubbling around the sides. Don't overcook or the noodles get soggy; finish under the broiler if the cheese isn't brown, and rest at least 15 minutes.

summary: Triple-smoky macaroni and cheese: elbows cooked just to al dente, a bechamel with smoked paprika, chipotle and rosemary melted with smoked cheddar and mozzarella, topped with garlicky homemade breadcrumbs and baked at 350°F about 30 minutes; serves 6-8 as a main.
glance: 350°F for about 30 minutes, until bubbling and the crumbs are browned
smoked cheddar, smoked paprika and chipotle
refrigerate before baking; add the breadcrumbs at the last minute and allow extra baking time
faq: How is the smoky flavor built?
Three layers: oak-smoked cheddar (or smoked mozzarella), smoked paprika and chipotle in adobo. The smoke is present but not overpowering, and a good match for a little chili heat.
Can I make a kid-friendly version?
The author made one big pot of bechamel and divided it before adding cheese and spices: the kid portion was straight cheddar and mozzarella, and it was darn good.
Why homemade breadcrumbs?

The canned ones are pretty awful, too powdery and flavorless, and homemade are a great way to use up stale bread. Mario Batali gave permission to leave the crust on; others consider that abhorrent. Saute them with garlic in butter until lightly browned.
How do I cook the macaroni?
Drain it when it is just becoming al dente, because it will bake more in the oven, and toss with 2 tablespoons butter.
How intense should the sauce be?
Pretty intense, because it will be diluted by a full pound of pasta. Taste and adjust the seasoning; it will probably need a little salt, depending on the cheeses.
Can I make it ahead?
Yes, refrigerate it, which is convenient for dinner parties. Wait to top with breadcrumbs until the last minute and allow additional baking time to come up to temperature.

summary: Shaved summer squash composed salad: summer squash, cucumber and Parmigiano shaved with a vegetable peeler, a quick-blanched carrot, sweet pepper and cherry tomatoes, dressed only with top-notch olive oil, lemon and Maldon salt and finished with thyme and squash blossom; serves 2 in 15 minutes.
glance: barely manipulate peak produce; dress only when plating
boiled until tender, then shocked in ice water
Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free (vegan without the cheese)
faq: Is this a recipe or a method?

The author says to think of it more as a method: be sensitive to the ingredients you have on hand and how you can cut and arrange them to emphasize their greatness, and it might be the showstopper of your meal.
How do I prepare the vegetables?

Shave the cucumber, summer squash and Parmigiano with a vegetable peeler or mandoline, quickly boil the carrot until tender when pierced and shock in ice water so its texture doesn't overwhelm the other ingredients, and slice the pepper and tomatoes.
When do I dress the salad?
Don't dress until you're ready to plate: toss only the cucumber and squash with a little olive oil, a squeeze of lemon and a big pinch of sea salt.
What dressing is used?
Just top-notch extra-virgin olive oil, lemon juice and Maldon salt.
What garnishes?
Shaved Parmigiano-Reggiano, fresh thyme leaves and a chiffonade of squash blossom.

summary: Spaghetti with fresh artichokes, recreated from The Pink Door in Seattle: trimmed baby, medium or large artichokes sliced 1/8 inch thin and sauteed on high heat about 15 minutes with garlic, tossed with spaghetti, pecorino romano and olive oil; serves 3-4.
glance: 16 baby, 8 medium or 4 large, sliced 1/8 inch thick
about 15 minutes, until tender with a hint of crunch and some browning
faq: How do I prepare baby artichokes?

For ones up to about 2 inches wide: cut off the top third, pull off dark green outer leaves until you reach yellowish ones, trim the very end of the stem, peel the stem and coarse base with a vegetable peeler, halve lengthwise, remove any hairy choke with a spoon and keep in acidulated water (water with a squeezed lemon).
How do I prepare larger artichokes?
Remove all the leaves, trim the stem end, pare away the coarse stuff around the base of the heart, peel the stem and thick skin, remove all the hairy choke with a spoon, and keep in acidulated water.
Should I keep the stems?
Yes, don't waste the stems, and don't quarter the artichokes: they get sliced thin.
How do I cook the artichokes?

Drain and pat dry thoroughly, slice about 1/8 inch thick, and saute in a few tablespoons of olive oil over high heat with a couple teaspoons of salt, tossing frequently, about 15 minutes, adding the garlic when they're close to done.
What flavors could I add?
Chili flakes, orange zest or fresh mint (added at the very end).
Where does the recipe come from?
The author and his wife loved the spaghetti with fresh artichokes at The Pink Door in Seattle and recreated it at home.

summary: Soba noodle soup in shiitake shoyu broth with asparagus, leeks and tofu: dried shiitake, kombu, ginger and garlic simmered 20 minutes, leeks added for 10 more, seasoned with shoyu and served over buckwheat noodles with 8-minute eggs, grilled asparagus, soft tofu and green onions; serves 4.
glance: 8 cups water, 2 cups dried shiitake and kombu simmered 20 minutes, leeks 10 more
cold water to a boil, covered off the heat for exactly 8 minutes
1 pound dry soba (extra, for a leftover soba pancake)
Vegetarian; vegan if you omit the eggs; not gluten-free
faq: What is soba?

A Japanese noodle made from buckwheat flour, often served cold with a dipping sauce but equally great in soup. The flavor is distinctively nutty and earthy; the author says it reminds him of the kasha his Eastern European Jewish family served. Ramen or udon would also work.
How do I make the umami-rich broth?

Rinse dried shiitakes and simmer them with kombu, ginger and garlic in 8 cups of water for 20 minutes, add the leeks for 10 more minutes, then strain, squeezing the mushrooms, and add 3 tablespoons of shoyu, tasting for more.
What is shoyu?

The Japanese name for soy sauce. The author loves Ohsawa Organic Unpasteurized Nama Shoyu, which he says is to most shoyu as parmigiano reggiano is to the stuff in the green can: more complex and caramelized, less salty, no chemical edge.
How do I cook the eggs?

Cover eggs with cold water by 1/2 inch, bring to a boil, then cover and remove from the heat. For soft-boiled use about 4 minutes, hard-boiled 12; here exactly 8 minutes, then shock in cold water. The whites and yolk are set, but the yolk is slightly underdone and translucent.
How do I cook the asparagus?
Brush with oil and grill in a single layer (a grill pan works) or cook in a large skillet until tender with charred spots.
Can I vary the toppings?
Yes, to suit your mood and the contents of your vegetable drawer. These toppings are a transition from winter (leeks, dried mushrooms) to spring (asparagus, eggs).

summary: King oyster mushroom lettuce wraps with ssamjang: halved king oyster mushrooms tossed in an ssamjang, mirin and sesame glaze and grilled until caramelized, wrapped in lettuce with warm rice, kaiware sprouts and minced kimchi; vegan, makes 8 wraps in 10 minutes plus rice time.
glance: 4 large king oyster, halved lengthwise, grilled until caramelized on both sides
1 tablespoon ssamjang in the glaze plus 1/4 cup for dipping
faq: What is ssamjang?

A crazy delicious Korean condiment made from fermented bean paste, chile paste and aromatics. The name literally means "wrapping sauce." Find it at Korean markets and online; here it's used both as a grilling sauce and for passing at the table.
Where do I find king oyster mushrooms?
At Korean markets, where they tend to be much less expensive than at fancy grocers. They are big, meaty mushrooms with a mild flavor that even people skeptical about wild mushrooms will enjoy.
How do I choose vegetarian kimchi?

Look closely at the ingredients: many kimchis include shrimp or other seafood, but vegetarian options exist. Explore different brands because they are not all the same; farmer's markets may have very fresh local varieties with more character.
How do I cook the mushrooms?

Whisk ssamjang with mirin, then vegetable oil, sesame oil, sugar and salt. Heat a grill pan or cast iron skillet to medium-high, toss the mushrooms with the sauce and cook until caramelized on one side, then turn and cook the other.
How do I assemble the wraps?

Put 1/4 cup of warm rice in the middle of a lettuce leaf and top with a mushroom half, kaiware and a couple teaspoons of minced kimchi. Diners roll up the leaves and dip in the ssamjang thinned with a little water.

summary: Warm fennel salad with pears and candied pumpkin seeds: thin-sliced fennel sauteed about 5 minutes, pear batons added for 2 minutes and tossed with cider vinegar, served on butter lettuce with crunchy cinnamon-sugar pumpkin seeds; vegan, serves 6.
glance: 1 head sliced 1/8 inch, sauteed about 5 minutes; pear cooked 2 more
1/2 cup toasted about 5 minutes, then caramelized with sugar, cinnamon and salt
faq: Why cook the fennel?
Cooking the fennel makes the taste milder and sweeter, so even people who don't enjoy the anise flavor may like it.
How do I make the candied pumpkin seeds?

Toast hulled green pumpkin seeds in a dry skillet about 5 minutes until fragrant, add 1 tablespoon sugar, a pinch of cinnamon and a big pinch of sea salt and keep cooking until the sugar melts and caramelizes, then turn out onto foil. They stick together; break them up by hand.
Are the pumpkin seeds safe to handle hot?

Melted sugar gives wicked burns, so be careful getting them out of the skillet and cool them thoroughly before handling. Consider a double batch since they tend to disappear and make killer cocktail snacks.
Can I change the seeds, fruit or cheese?
Spice the seeds with cumin, ancho chili powder or smoked paprika; use apple instead of pear; add a bit of goat cheese or gorgonzola.
What pear should I use?
A ripe variety that is eaten firm, cut into 1/4-inch batons.

summary: Spicy and seedy Indian potatoes, a dry-fried side: onion, garlic and cubed waxy potatoes browned then simmered covered in 1/2 cup water until just tender and cooked dry, finished with toasted sesame, fennel, coriander and mustard seeds, ginger, lime juice, cilantro and green onions; serves 4-6.
glance: 2 pounds waxy or medium-waxy (Yukon Gold or All-Red) in 1/2-inch cubes
5 minutes browning, then simmer covered until just tender; cook off the liquid
sesame, fennel, coriander and black mustard, toasted about 2 minutes
faq: What are dry-fried Indian vegetables?

Indian food in American restaurants is so driven by saucy curries that we miss out on dry-fried spicy vegetables. This potato dish might not be precisely traditional in flavors or technique but works with any Indian meal.
Why add most of the spices at the end?
To really make the flavors pop: most of the spices, along with lime juice and fresh ginger, go in right at the end, for contrasting bright notes against the mellow, earthy potatoes.
How do I keep the potatoes from turning to mash?

Stop cooking at the right point, when the potatoes are tender but still cubes. Control the liquid during the last few minutes: add a little water as needed while covered, and uncover to cook off excess liquid.
What potatoes should I use?
Any small, waxy or medium-waxy potatoes, or a mix; Yukon Golds are great and easy to find. The author used All-Reds, which are pink all the way through.
How do I make them less spicy?
Tone down the chili flakes and jalapeno to taste.
How can I serve leftovers?
The author ate them four days straight: hot, cold, with yogurt, with Tapatio; also good with a fried egg on top or in a tortilla.

summary: Cold sorrel and coconut milk soup: sorrel just barely wilted 30 seconds with onion, blended with a can of coconut milk and ginger for 2 minutes, strained through a fine sieve and chilled, garnished with cucumber and red onion; vegan, serves 2 or more as an amuse-bouche.
glance: 2 (easily multiplied), or more as an amuse-bouche
4 ounces leaves and tender stems, wilted about 30 seconds
one 13.5-ounce can, preferably without thickeners or gums
faq: What does sorrel taste like?
The wilted sorrel's lemony flavor was so refreshing that the author felt cognitive dissonance tasting it hot and realized it wanted to be a cold soup.
Do I have to cook the sorrel?
The author has only made it once with cooked sorrel, but suspects that skipping the cooking would be fine and probably give a nicer color.
How do I get a velvety texture?

The difference between good and great in pureed soups: run the blender a good long time to reduce the particle size (2 minutes on maximum, with the vent open and covered with a towel), then strain first through a coarse sieve and then your finest sieve, or use a fine chinois.
Why coconut milk instead of cream?
The author stuck with coconut milk, pureed it and limited the flavoring to just a bit of fresh ginger. It was an idea that started as an Indian-style soup with sorrel in place of spinach.
How do I garnish it?
Just before serving, taste and adjust seasoning, divide among chilled bowls and garnish with finely diced cucumber and red onion mixed together and a few flakes of Maldon salt.

summary: A "rice bowl" template, inspired by bibimbap: short-grain rice topped with separately pan-fried tofu and vegetables, fresh salad items and a quick sauce or spice paste, arranged and garnished; serves 4 and adaptable to any season or cuisine.
glance: 2.5 cups short-grain (like Niko Niko or Thai Jasmine)
1.5 pounds tofu, or 1 pound tempeh, seitan or vegetarian sausage
cooked rice, 1-2 pan-fried vegetables, 4 handfuls of fresh salad items, a sauce, garnishes
faq: What is a rice bowl?

The author's family name for an improvisational dish inspired by Korean bi-bim-bap: short-grain rice, a few sauteed ingredients, a few fresh vegetables and a quick sauce, arranged attractively. The noodle version, inspired by Vietnamese bun, is called a noodle bowl.
Why keep each item separate?
You can control how each one is cooked and seasoned for maximum flavor, and it's still attainable as a weeknight supper.
How do I choose combinations?
Adapt it to any ingredients in any season as long as you think about flavor combinations: when in doubt, stick to things you've seen paired before or that are common in a cuisine you like.
What is the example's sauce?
A rough paste pounded in a mortar and pestle from Thai chilis, garlic, green onion, sesame seed, cilantro, salt, pepper and lime juice. A bottled sauce such as sweet chili sauce works well.
How do I cook the protein and vegetables?
Slice the protein thinly and pan fry in a little oil until brown, season with salt. Individually pan fry the vegetables, seasoning with salt and pepper or a little soy sauce.
How do I assemble the bowl?

About 1 cup of cooked rice in the bottom, salad items around it, cooked protein and vegetables on top, then sauce and garnishes like toasted sesame seeds, citrus zest, crisped garlic or green onions, or a sunny-side-up egg bi-bim-bap style.
